The GAO released a formal framework last year for defining and detecting foreign state disinformation (GAO-24-107600). It is, by government standards, a serious piece of work. Now let's talk about what comes next, because the framework itself tells you something about where this is heading that the document doesn't quite say out loud. First, the obvious: the fact that the U.S. government needed a formal definitional baseline in 2024 reflects how far behind the institutional response has been. Russia has been running coordinated information operations against Western audiences since at least the 2014 annexation of Crimea. China's external influence apparatus, from the United Front Work Department to the hundreds of fake local news sites identified in the Dragonbridge investigations, has been operating at scale for nearly a decade. The GAO is not early to this. Nobody should mistake a taxonomy document for a capability. That said, the framework matters. Here's the part that deserves attention. The report draws a clean line between foreign government attribution and everything else, which sounds obvious but has enormous downstream consequences. Once you formally distinguish state-sponsored disinformation from domestic misinformation or private-actor manipulation, you've also delineated different legal authorities, different agency responsibilities, and different thresholds for response. That line will be contested. It already is. The adversaries who've read the room, and they have, know that the seam between "foreign" and "domestic" is where operations go to survive. This is not theoretical. The most durable Russian operations of the 2016-2020 period weren't the loud stuff. They were the ones that seeded content into genuine domestic political networks, waited for American users to amplify it organically, and then became effectively unattributable under any reasonable legal standard. The GRU's Internet Research Agency operation worked in part because it cultivated real Americans as unwitting distributors. By the time content reaches its third or fourth domestic amplifier, the foreign-origin question gets genuinely murky, and the GAO's framework, for all its utility, largely punts on that problem. It documents the gap. It does not close it. So watch for the next evolution. Attribution-resistant seeding into domestic networks will become more deliberate and more patient. The operational signature that analysts currently use to identify state-sponsored campaigns, the tell-tale patterns of coordinated inauthentic behavior, the linguistic artifacts, the off-hours posting patterns, the account age distribution, will be systematically sanded down. Not because adversaries fear the GAO's definitions, but because formal frameworks create formal detection thresholds, and detection thresholds are an operational target. The Chinese operations documented in the report deserve specific note here because their tradecraft trajectory is different from Russia's and is heading somewhere particular. Dragonbridge, which Meta, Google, and independent researchers have tracked extensively, has historically been noisy and low-engagement. Thousands of accounts producing content almost nobody read or shared. That looks like failure. It probably isn't. It looks more like a long-running calibration exercise, testing infrastructure, testing content resonance across different communities, mapping which narratives get traction and which don't. The operational output has been poor. The intelligence collection on American audience behavior has been extensive. The next iteration will be quieter and better aimed. The interagency coordination section of the GAO report is where I'd direct anyone who wants to understand the structural vulnerability. The report documents, carefully and in bureaucratic language, that agencies do not share threat information effectively. The State Department's Global Engagement Center, the FBI's Foreign Influence Task Force, the intelligence community's various foreign malign influence efforts, CISA's election security work: these operate with persistent friction between them, and some of that friction is legal (different authorities, different classification levels, different mandates regarding U.S. persons) and some of it is just organizational. The adversary operates across all of those seams simultaneously. The response apparatus is divided by them. Congress gets a clean evidence base from this report for statutory reform of counter-disinformation authorities. Whether they use it is a different question entirely, and the current political environment around anything labeled "disinformation" makes that legislatively treacherous. The word has become contested in ways that would have seemed strange five years ago. That contestation is not entirely organic, which anyone who's followed the GEC's budget fights on the Hill over the past two years should already suspect. What officials should actually watch between now and the 2026 midterms: Localized targeting will intensify. The shift toward state and local information environments, county election offices, local news deserts, city council races in competitive districts, has been documented in multiple election cycles now. The GAO framework is built primarily around federal-level threats and federal-level detection. State and local officials have almost no counter-disinformation capacity. That's a gap that will be used. Generative AI hasn't fully arrived in these operations yet. The content quality of identified Chinese and Russian operations has historically been identifiable, partly by its strange, slightly-off quality. That friction is disappearing. The volume-and-scatter approach that characterized Dragonbridge will become cheaper and more linguistically plausible. Detection methods that relied on linguistic artifacts are already degrading. The definition of "foreign government attribution" will be stress-tested through cutouts. State-sponsored actors will increasingly route operations through nominally private entities, commercial platforms, or third-country infrastructure specifically because the GAO framework, and the legal authorities that flow from it, require that attribution to trigger a response. If you can't attribute it to a foreign government, it falls into a legal and jurisdictional gray zone. The adversary playbook for the next cycle will be built around manufacturing that ambiguity. For voters and civil society: the GAO framework is a useful reference document. It is not protection. The operations it documents were effective precisely because they worked through content that felt locally resonant and was shared by real people. Platform labels, media literacy campaigns, and government attribution announcements are downstream of the infection. By the time you're reading the State Department's foreign attribution press release, the narrative has already been circulating for months. The posture that actually helps is skepticism toward sudden, emotionally intense information that confirms existing grievances and arrives through informal networks. That's not a satisfying answer. MDPI just published an encyclopedic reference entry on state disinformation, tracing the operational lineage from Soviet "disinformatsiya" through today's coordinated inauthentic behavior networks. It's a solid synthesis. It's also, if you read it carefully, a roadmap of where the next phase is already heading. The entry does the definitional work most public debate skips. Disinformation, misinformation, propaganda, malinformation. These aren't synonyms with different vibes. They map to different legal regimes, different attribution standards, different platform liability frameworks. The people running influence operations in Moscow and Beijing absolutely understand this distinction. A lot of legislators writing counter-disinformation law still don't, which is a problem we'll return to. Here's what the historical arc in this entry actually tells us about trajectory. The KGB's Service A ran active measures on timelines measured in months or years. Fabricate a document, plant it in a Nairobi newspaper, let it migrate to European outlets, watch it surface in a parliamentary debate. Slow, labor-intensive, plausibly deniable. The digital transition didn't just speed this up. It changed the economics so radically that the operational logic flipped. When distribution is essentially free and amplification can be outsourced to the algorithm, the incentive shifts away from the single high-craft forgery toward volume, velocity, and disposability. Flood the zone. Make the correction chase the lie. That transition is documented. What the encyclopedic framing captures but doesn't fully stress is that we're now entering a third phase, and defenders are still mostly organized around the second one. Phase two, the IRA era, was characterized by coordinated inauthentic behavior: networks of fake accounts, sockpuppets, troll farms with org charts and shift schedules. The St. Petersburg Internet Research Agency had a building. It had HR. Researchers and platform trust-and-safety teams got reasonably good at identifying this infrastructure because infrastructure leaves traces. Accounts that post at odd hours relative to their claimed location. Engagement patterns that cluster unnaturally. Profile creation dates that bunch suspiciously. None of this is easy, but it's tractable. The coming phase is harder to see coming precisely because it doesn't require a building. Generative AI drops the production cost of synthetic content to something close to zero. Not just text. Convincing audio, images, video. The fabricated document that Service A spent weeks constructing in 1976 can now be produced in an afternoon by someone who isn't a professional forger and doesn't need to be. More importantly, it can be produced at scale. Not one planted story. Ten thousand micro-targeted variants, each slightly tuned to the specific anxieties of a specific community in a specific media ecosystem. The IRA model was centralized because centralization was necessary. You needed people in a room coordinating the messaging. Generative tools allow genuine decentralization. A state actor can seed a narrative and let a diffuse network of loosely affiliated, not-formally-recruited amplifiers run with it. Attribution becomes nightmarish. Was that Facebook group pushing the fabricated story about a candidate's health record a GRU front, or was it three guys in Ohio who got played? The operational answer may be: both, and the state doesn't much care which. The entry's breakdown of distinct actor profiles is worth reading against this trajectory. Russia's model, IRA plus GRU Unit 54777, is the most documented. The innovation Russia brought to the Soviet playbook was speed and emotional targeting. Not ideological persuasion. Amplifying existing divisions, making people angry, making them distrust institutions. The goal isn't to convince you Russia is right. The goal is to convince you that nothing is trustworthy, including the people telling you Russia is running influence operations. China's model is structurally different and in some ways more ambitious. The domestic censorship architecture, the Great Firewall, is fundamentally defensive: keep foreign narratives out. The external projection arm, Xinhua, CGTN, the overseas Chinese-language media ecosystem, state-affiliated content farms, is offensive but also more interested in agenda-setting than acute destabilization. China generally doesn't want Western democracies in chaos. It wants them distracted, divided on values questions, and deferential on economic ones. The interference around Taiwan, around Xinjiang coverage, around Hong Kong, has been remarkably consistent in its actual content goals even as the delivery mechanisms have evolved. Iran targets diaspora communities with a specificity that's often underappreciated in Western coverage. The operations around the 2020 U.S. election, documented in detail by Meta and Microsoft, involved spoofed email addresses and fabricated content designed to intimidate specific voter populations. Iran also runs a version of the hack-and-leak playbook, sometimes in coordination with North Korea's more purely criminal hacking operations. The IRGC's cyber units have gotten considerably better at this over the past five years. North Korea is the entry's most compressed treatment, and honestly that's fair. Pyongyang's disinformation capacity is mostly in service of financial operations and targeted harassment of defectors and journalists, not large-scale democratic interference. The tradecraft overlap with state-sponsored cybercrime is significant. Now, what should people actually watch for. For defenders: the definitional distinctions the entry makes matter enormously for what tools you're allowed to use. Counter-disinformation that conflates true-but-misleadingly-deployed content (malinformation) with fabricated content (disinformation) will keep losing in court and in public legitimacy battles. The EU's FIMI framework is more rigorous on this than most U.S. legislative proposals. American counter-influence architecture is still largely built around the Cold War model of public exposure, the Active Measures Working Group approach, which works when the operation is visible enough to expose. It works less well against diffuse, decentralized, AI-assisted operations where there's no single GRU officer to name. The fundamental tension the entry identifies, exposing disinformation versus amplifying it by talking about it, hasn't been resolved in 40 years of serious thinking. It probably won't be resolved. But the calculus is shifting. In an environment where fabricated content reaches millions before any correction exists, the exposure penalty is smaller relative to the non-exposure penalty than it used to be. The case for faster, louder exposure is getting stronger. The case for quiet behind-the-scenes platform coordination is getting weaker as platforms themselves become less reliable partners. For election officials specifically: the next phase of targeting is probably going to be operational rather than persuasive. Not trying to change minds about candidates. Trying to disrupt the process itself. Fabricated guidance about polling locations or ID requirements, synthetic audio of election officials saying things they didn't say, influence operations targeting election workers to drive them out of their jobs through harassment. The 2024 cycle globally showed some early versions of this. The 2026 midterms and the broader run of elections in Germany, France, Australia, Canada over the next 18 months are going to be stress tests. For voters and citizens, the news is uncomfortable. The reliable tell of influence operation content, that it came from an obviously fake account or an obviously foreign source, is going away. The synthetic content that's coming will be produced with domestic aesthetics, will reference local concerns, will not have a St. Petersburg IP address baked in. The epistemological challenge here is real and I won't pretend there's a clean consumer-level fix. Slowing down before sharing, checking whether a piece of audio or video has been verified by someone with actual access to the subject, being specifically skeptical of content that makes you feel a strong emotional reaction right before an election. None of this is sufficient. But the alternative, which is treating your current epistemic habits as adequate for the next five years of this, is worse. The encyclopedic entry documents where we've been with real rigor. The trajectory it implies is one where the question isn't whether state actors will adopt generative tools at scale. They already are. The question is whether democratic institutions will reorganize fast enough to deal with operations that no longer require the infrastructure that made the last generation of interference legible and attributable.
